beats.intro: Chapter four. [[sub]]A forecast is a model of the future, built from the statements of the past. This chapter shows how to build one, and how to stop yourself fooling yourself.
beats.model: A sales-based model starts at the top line. [[rev]]Say revenue grows eight percent, to one thousand eighty. [[cogs]]Cost of sales is sixty percent of revenue: six forty eight. Gross profit, four thirty two. [[sga]]Selling and administration is twenty five percent: two seventy. EBIT, one sixty two. [[int]]Interest is thirty, tax is thirty percent of what is left, and net income is ninety two point four. [[eps]]Divide by one hundred shares and earnings per share is zero point nine two. [[note]]Every line follows from a few assumptions. Change an assumption and the whole forecast moves.
beats.revenue: Revenue itself comes from volume and price. [[a]]Product A sells one hundred units at ten pounds. Volume grows ten percent, price three percent, so revenue rises from one thousand to eleven thirty three. [[b]]Product B holds volume flat, but raises price five percent. Revenue goes from one thousand to ten fifty. [[tot]]The total moves from two thousand to twenty one eighty three. Forecasting each driver separately shows where growth really comes from.
beats.cashflow: The income statement feeds the rest of the model. [[ebit]]Start with EBIT of one sixty two. [[tax]]Remove tax at thirty percent: one thirteen point four. [[da]]Add back depreciation of fifty, which is not a cash cost. [[capex]]Subtract capital spending of seventy, and an increase in working capital of twenty. [[fcff]]What remains is free cash flow to the firm: seventy three point four. That is the cash a valuation model discounts.
beats.scenarios: One forecast is one guess. [[base]]In a case study for Rémy Cointreau, the base case put free cash flow in 2024 at three hundred million euros. [[alt]]Two reasonable alternatives, changing only sales growth, margin and working capital, gave one twenty nine, and one hundred five. [[note]]The range of outcomes is far wider than any single number. Building scenarios is how an analyst shows that honestly.
beats.biases: Five behavioral biases bend forecasts. Each has a remedy. [[b1]]Overconfidence: faith in your own accuracy. Record and review forecasts, and use scenarios. [[b2]]Illusion of control: believing more data and more complex models always help. Model only the few variables that matter. [[b3]]Conservatism: clinging to old views. Have forecasts reviewed by others, and test management guidance as a scenario. [[b4]]Representativeness: forcing new facts into old categories. Start from the industry base rate, then adjust. [[b5]]Confirmation: seeking only supporting evidence. Study competitors, substitutes, and people who disagree.
beats.forces: How much can a company charge, and what will its inputs cost? Porter's five forces help. [[center]]At the center, rivalry among existing competitors. [[four]]Around it: the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, the bargaining power of buyers, and the bargaining power of suppliers. [[strong]]When these forces are weak, the company has pricing power, and can protect margins. [[weak]]When they are strong, prices fall and costs rise, and margins are squeezed. Forecast prices and costs accordingly.
beats.inflation: Inflation hits revenue and costs differently. [[base]]Start with a price of one hundred, and a unit cost of sixty. The margin is forty. [[cost]]Now input costs rise ten percent, to sixty six. [[strong]]A strong brand passes it all on. Price rises to one ten, and the margin grows to forty four. [[weak]]A weak competitor can pass on only four percent. Price one oh four, margin thirty eight, a thinner margin. [[note]]So forecast inflation separately for sales and for costs, and judge how much each company can pass on.
beats.horizon: How far should the explicit forecast run? [[factors]]It depends on the investment horizon, the cyclicality of the industry, company-specific events such as a restructuring, and sometimes the employer's rules. [[cycle]]The period should be long enough for the business to reach mid-cycle, or normalized, earnings. [[tv]]Beyond that horizon, a terminal value captures everything later, usually by assuming a long-run growth rate or an exit multiple. [[note]]Normalized earnings stop a temporary peak or trough from being projected forever.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]A sales-based model flows from revenue drivers, through margins, to earnings and free cash flow. [[w2]]Build scenarios, because one forecast is one guess. [[w3]]Know your biases: overconfidence, illusion of control, conservatism, representativeness and confirmation. [[w4]]Competitive position and inflation shape prices and costs, and the horizon should reach normalized earnings.
